title: Paper 1: Applications of Mathematical Knowledge
target_note: Harder than Mock A on purpose, and harder in the way the real test is: no question needs anything beyond the specification, and most have an obvious method that will not fit in the time. A 7+ candidate should expect to leave two or three and still finish.

questions.stem_html:
Solve 9x + 27 = 4 × 3x+1.

What is the sum of the solutions?
questions.solution_html:
Write everything in powers of 3. The trap is on the right: 4 × 3x+1 = 4 × 3 × 3x = 12 × 3x, not 4 × 3x.

With t = 3x: t2 − 12t + 27 = 0, so (t − 3)(t − 9) = 0 and t = 3 or 9.

Then x = 1 or x = 2, and the sum is 3.

Both roots are positive, so neither is lost — but check that habit anyway: t = 3x can never be negative, and on a different quadratic that is the whole question.

traps.A: One of the two solutions, not the sum.
traps.C: Reading 4 × 3ˣ⁺¹ as 4 × 3ˣ, which gives t² − 4t + 27 = 0 and no real roots — then answering anyway.
traps.D: Doubling the larger solution, or adding 4 and 2.
traps.E: The sum of the two values of t (3 + 9), not of x.

questions.stem_html:
x > 1 and

log3 x + logx 3 = 52.

What is the product of the possible values of x?
questions.solution_html:
logx 3 is the reciprocal of log3 x. That one line is the whole question.

Let u = log3 x. Then u + 1u = 52, so 2u2 − 5u + 2 = 0 and u = 2 or 12.

So x = 32 = 9 or x = 31/2 = √3, and the product is 9√3.

Or skip the values entirely: the product is 3u₁ × 3u₂ = 3u₁+u₂, and the sum of the roots is 52 by inspection. 35/2 = 9√3 in one step.

traps.A: Dividing 9 by 2 rather than multiplying 9 by √3.
traps.B: 3^(3/2). Comes from taking the sum of the roots as 3/2 rather than 5/2.
traps.C: Only one of the two values.
traps.D: The sum of the two values of x, not their product.
traps.F: 3³ — adding the exponents as 2 + 1 instead of 2 + ½.

questions.stem_html:
How many integers k are there for which

x2 + kx + 36 = 0

has two distinct integer roots?
questions.solution_html:
If the roots are p and q then pq = 36 and k = −(p + q).

Positive factor pairs of 36: (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9), (6, 6). The negatives of each pair work too, since (−p)(−q) = 36.

Distinct rules out (6, 6).

That leaves four pairs, each giving a k and its negative: k = ±13, ±15, ±20, ±37 — 8 values.

The word doing the work is 'distinct'. Without it the answer is 10, which is sitting in the options waiting.

traps.B: One stray value has crept in, usually k = −12 counted once.
traps.C: The answer to this question without the word 'distinct': (6, 6) adds k = ±12.
traps.D: Counting the divisors of 36 rather than the factor pairs.
traps.E: Counting ordered pairs (p, q) rather than values of k — each pair and its reverse give the same k.

questions.stem_html:
The cubic p(x) = x3 + ax2 + bx + c has three roots which are consecutive integers, and p(0) = −6.

What is a + b + c?
questions.solution_html:
The fast route never finds a, b or c at all.

p(1) = 1 + a + b + c. So if 1 is a root, a + b + c = −1 immediately.

And 1 is a root: with roots n−1, n, n+1 we have p(0) = −(n−1)n(n+1) = −6, so n(n2−1) = 6, giving n = 2 and roots 1, 2, 3.

Hence a + b + c = −1.

Expanding (x−1)(x−2)(x−3) to get a = −6, b = 11, c = −6 and then adding is perfectly correct and costs you two minutes you did not have.

traps.A: That is c on its own, or a on its own — both are −6.
traps.C: Zero is what you get if you set p(1) = 1 rather than 0.
traps.D: Sign slip: p(1) = 0 gives 1 + a + b + c = 0, so the sum is −1, not +1.
traps.E: The product of the roots, or −c.
traps.F: That is b on its own.

questions.stem_html:
The circle C has equation x2 + y2 − 2x = 0.

For how many values of m is the line y = mx + 4 a tangent to C?
questions.solution_html:
C is (x−1)2 + y2 = 1: centre (1, 0), radius 1. The point (0, 4) is at distance √17 from the centre, so it lies outside, and from an external point there are two tangents.

But one of them is the vertical line x = 0, whose distance from (1, 0) is exactly 1. A vertical line has no gradient, so it is not of the form y = mx + 4.

That leaves 1 value of m. (Solving properly: |m + 4| = √m2+1 gives m = −158.)

Every instinct says 2, and the geometry agrees — it is the parametrisation that loses one. Any question asking 'how many values of m' rather than 'how many tangents' is asking exactly this.

traps.A: There is one; the point (0,4) is outside the circle, not inside it.
traps.C: Two tangents exist, but one is vertical and so has no value of m.
traps.D: Three is the count of common tangents to two circles, not this.
traps.F: Only a degenerate circle would give infinitely many.

questions.stem_html:
Evaluate

1√2 + 1 + 1√3 + √2 + … + 1√25 + √24

(that is, the sum of 1/(√r+1 + √r) for r = 1 to 24).
questions.solution_html:
Rationalise one term and the sum collapses:

1√r+1 + √r = √r+1 − √r.

(Multiply top and bottom by √r+1 − √r; the denominator becomes (r+1) − r = 1.)

Every middle term cancels, leaving √25 − √1 = 5 − 1 = 4.

Adding the 24 terms on a calculator is not available to you and would not be faster if it were. The rationalising step is the only route in.

traps.A: A halving that comes from rationalising a difference of squares that is not there.
traps.B: This is what you get rationalising the wrong way round, giving √r − √(r+1).
traps.D: √24 is the last term's index, not the sum.
traps.E: √25 on its own — the −√1 at the start of the telescope is still there.
traps.F: The number of terms, not their sum.

questions.stem_html:
What is the coefficient of x4 in the expansion of

(1 + x + x2)5?
questions.solution_html:
The binomial theorem does not apply directly — three terms, not two. Two ways in, and only one is quick.

Write 1 + x + x2 = 1 − x31 − x. Then the expansion is (1 − x3)5(1 − x)−5.

For x4: take x0 from the first bracket and x4 from the second, or x3 from the first and x1 from the second.

(1 − x)−5 has xj coefficient j+4C4. So the answer is 1 × 8C4 − 5 × 5C4 = 70 − 25 = 45.

Multiplying (1+x+x2) by itself five times is the obvious route and takes about four minutes. It is also the route most likely to drop a term.

traps.A: Counts only the arrangements using two x² terms.
traps.B: One of the three families of terms contributing to x⁴ is missing.
traps.C: Drops the correction term entirely — this is ⁸C₄ with an arithmetic slip.
traps.D: 70 − 25 done wrong; the method is right.
traps.F: Double counting: 2 × 40, or ⁸C₄ plus its own correction instead of minus.

questions.stem_html:
The points A(3, 4) and B(−4, 3) both lie on the circle x2 + y2 = 25.

What is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the chord AB?
questions.solution_html:
Both points are on the circle, so the perpendicular from the centre bisects AB — and its foot is the midpoint.

Midpoint of AB is (−12, 72).

Distance from the origin: √14 + 494 = √504 = 5√22.

Finding the equation of AB and using the point-to-line formula gets the same answer and takes three times as long. The midpoint shortcut only exists because both points are on the circle.

traps.B: √2 is the square root of the midpoint's x-coordinate squared, doubled — a slip.
traps.C: Half the radius — true only if the chord subtended 120°, which it does not.
traps.E: 5 is the radius, the distance to the circle itself, not to the chord.
traps.F: 25/2 is the square of the distance, not the distance.

questions.detail: Distance from centre to a chord

questions.stem_html:
How many lines are tangent to both of the circles

x2 + y2 = 9 and (x − 5)2 + y2 = 4?
questions.solution_html:
Centres (0, 0) and (5, 0); radii 3 and 2. The distance between the centres is 5.

3 + 2 = 5, so the circles touch externally at exactly one point.

Two circles that touch externally have 3 common tangents: two external ones, and the single line through the point of contact.

The arithmetic is trivial and the whole question is whether you notice that d = r1 + r2 exactly. One unit either way and the answer is 4 or 2.

traps.A: Zero applies when one circle lies strictly inside the other.
traps.B: One applies when the circles touch internally.
traps.C: Two applies when the circles properly overlap — here they only touch.
traps.E: Four applies when the circles are fully separate; here d is exactly r₁ + r₂, not more.
traps.F: Only identical circles would give infinitely many.

questions.stem_html:
How many solutions does

sin 3x = sin x

have for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
questions.solution_html:
Do not expand sin 3x. Use the difference:

sin 3x − sin x = 2 cos 2x sin x = 0.

sin x = 0 gives x = 0, π, 2π — three solutions, and both endpoints count because the interval is closed.

cos 2x = 0 gives 2x = π2, 3π2, 5π2, 7π2, so x = π4, 3π4, 5π4, 7π4 — four more.

Total 7.

Expanding sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin3x also works and takes far longer. The endpoints are where the marks are lost either way.

traps.A: Four counts only the cos 2x family.
traps.B: Five usually means one endpoint was dropped from the sin x family.
traps.C: Six is the answer on the open interval 0 < x < 2π — the interval here is closed.
traps.E: Eight double-counts one of the endpoints.
traps.F: Nine counts 2x-values rather than x-values somewhere in the cos 2x family.

questions.detail: Counting solutions of a trigonometric equation

questions.stem_html:
A triangle has sides of length 13, 14 and 15.

What is the radius of its inscribed circle?
questions.solution_html:
Semi-perimeter s = 13 + 14 + 152 = 21.

Heron: area = √21 × 8 × 7 × 6 = √7056 = 84.

The incircle touches all three sides, so the triangle splits into three triangles of heights r: area = rs.

Hence r = 8421 = 4.

13-14-15 is the standard 'nice' triangle precisely because Heron gives a whole number. Recognising it saves the minute you would spend checking the arithmetic.

traps.B: Area over perimeter rather than area over semi-perimeter, then halved again.
traps.E: 84 ÷ 14, using a side length instead of the semi-perimeter.
traps.F: One of Heron's factors (s − 13 = 8), not the radius.

questions.stem_html:
A sector of a circle has radius r and angle θ radians. Its perimeter — two radii plus the arc — is 20.

What is the largest possible area of the sector?
questions.solution_html:
Perimeter: 2r + rθ = 20, so θ = 20 − 2rr.

Area = 12r2θ = 12r(20 − 2r) = 10r − r2.

That is a downward parabola in r, greatest at r = 5, giving area 50 − 25 = 25.

The θ disappears the moment you substitute, and with it any need for calculus — completing the square on 10r − r2 is faster than differentiating. At r = 5, θ = 2 radians, which is a perfectly ordinary sector.

traps.A: The area at r = 2 — a valid sector, just not the largest.
traps.B: Maximising with θ fixed at 2π/3 rather than letting it vary.
traps.D: The area at r = 3 or r = 7, either side of the maximum.
traps.E: The area at r = 4 or r = 6 — very close, and the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.stem_html:
f(x) = x3 − 3x.

How many distinct real solutions does f(f(x)) = 0 have?
questions.solution_html:
f(x) = 0 when x(x2−3) = 0, so x = 0, ±√3.

So f(f(x)) = 0 needs f(x) = 0, √3 or −√3.

Now the shape. f′(x) = 3x2 − 3, so there is a local maximum at (−1, 2) and a local minimum at (1, −2). The line y = c therefore meets the curve three times whenever |c| < 2.

|0| < 2 and √3 ≈ 1.73 < 2, so all three equations have three roots each: 9 in total, and they are distinct because the three values of c are.

The entire question is whether √3 < 2. If the cubic had been x3 − 3x with roots at ±√3 but a turning value of 1, the answer would be 5.

traps.A: Three is the number of roots of f(x) = 0, not of f(f(x)) = 0.
traps.B: Five is the answer if √3 were greater than the turning value of 2 — check it.
traps.C: Six counts only two of the three families.
traps.D: Seven would need one family to give a repeated root; none does.
traps.F: 27 is 3³, the answer if every root split into three again indefinitely.

questions.stem_html: What is the total area of the region enclosed between the curve y = x3 − x and the x-axis?
questions.solution_html:
The curve cuts the axis at x = −1, 0, 1, making two loops.

Between 0 and 1 the curve is below the axis; between −1 and 0 it is above. By symmetry the two loops have equal area.

One loop: ∫01(x − x3) dx = [x22 − x44]01 = 12 − 14 = 14.

Total = 2 × 14 = 12.

∫−11(x3−x) dx = 0, because the curve is odd and the loops cancel. 'Area' is never the signed integral across a root.

traps.A: The signed integral from −1 to 1 — the two loops cancel. Area does not cancel.
traps.D: 3/4 comes from integrating x − x³ over the whole of [−1, 1] without splitting.
traps.E: 1 is four quarter-loops — there are only two loops.
traps.F: 2 is the width of the interval, not an area.

questions.stem_html: How many tangents to the curve y = x3 − 3x pass through the point (0, 2)?
questions.solution_html:
The tangent at x = a has gradient 3a2 − 3 and passes through (a, a3 − 3a).

Through (0, 2):

2 = (3a2 − 3)(0 − a) + a3 − 3a = −2a3.

So a3 = −1, and a cube root is unique over the reals: a = −1. Exactly 1 tangent.

Everything about the question suggests 3 — it is a cubic, and (0, 2) is the local maximum value. But the tangency condition collapses to a3 = −1, which has one real root and two complex ones. Note (0,2) lies on the curve's local maximum height, which is what makes the algebra collapse so far.

traps.A: There is one — the tangent at x = −1, which is the horizontal line y = 2.
traps.C: Two would need a³ = −1 to have two real roots; it has one.
traps.D: Three is the instinctive answer for a cubic, and the one the question is built to catch.
traps.E: Four is not reachable from a cubic equation in a.
traps.F: Only a straight line would have infinitely many tangents through a point.

questions.detail: How many tangents pass through a point

questions.stem_html:
The curve y = f(x) has a minimum point at (1, −2).

The curve y = 2f(3 − x) − 1 has a stationary point. Where is it, and what kind of point is it?
questions.solution_html:
Read 3 − x as −(x − 3). The stationary point is where the input to f equals 1: 3 − x = 1, so x = 2.

The height: 2 × (−2) − 1 = −5.

Now the nature, which is the whole question. f(3−x) is f reflected in a vertical line — left and right are swapped, up and down are not. A valley reflected sideways is still a valley. The outer ×2 stretches it and the −1 lowers it; neither turns it over, because 2 is positive.

So it is a minimum at (2, −5).

Only a negative multiplier outside f turns a minimum into a maximum. The minus inside acts on x and does nothing to the nature of the point — which is exactly why this looks like a maximum at a glance.

traps.B: The minus is inside f, so it reflects left-to-right. Only a negative multiplier outside f would flip a minimum into a maximum.
traps.C: x = 4 comes from solving 3 − x = −1, or from reading the transformation as x − 3.
traps.D: x = −2 comes from treating 3 − x as a translation by 3 after the reflection, in the wrong order.
traps.E: −3 applies the −1 before the ×2 rather than after.
traps.F: Both coordinates and the nature are wrong — this is the every-slip-at-once option.

questions.detail: A reflection preserves the nature of a turning point

questions.stem_html:
How many real values of x satisfy

|x − 1| + |x − 3| = 2|x − 2|?
questions.solution_html:
Split at the three critical points and check each region.

For x ≤ 1: left = (1−x) + (3−x) = 4 − 2x; right = 2(2−x) = 4 − 2x. Equal for every such x.

For 1 < x < 3: left = 2 always; right = 2|x−2|, which is less than 2 except at the ends. No solutions strictly inside.

For x ≥ 3: left = (x−1) + (x−3) = 2x − 4; right = 2(x−2) = 2x − 4. Equal again.

So the solution set is x ≤ 1 together with x ≥ 3 — infinitely many values.

Every habit says an equation in one unknown has finitely many solutions. Here two of the three regions give identities, and you only see it by actually evaluating a region rather than solving it.

traps.A: There are solutions — every x ≤ 1 is one.
traps.B: One is what you get by only checking the middle region and finding an endpoint.
traps.C: Two comes from treating each outer region as giving a single boundary solution.
traps.D: Three counts the critical points 1, 2, 3, but x = 2 is not a solution.
traps.E: Four counts boundary cases rather than the intervals themselves.

questions.detail: An identity disguised as an equation

questions.stem_html:
In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA, and N lies on OB with ON : NB = 1 : 2.

AN and BM meet at P.

What is AP : PN?
questions.solution_html:
Take O as origin, with OA = a and OB = b. Then M = 12a and N = 13b.

A point on AN: a + t(13b − a).

A point on BM: b + s(12a − b).

Comparing coefficients: 1 − t = s2 and t3 = 1 − s.

Substituting gives t = 35, so AP : PN = t : (1 − t) = 35 : 25 = 3 : 2.

Two equations, two unknowns, and the answer is the parameter itself — there is no need to find P's position at all. Coordinates with specific numbers for a and b work equally well and are often faster under pressure.

traps.A: The ratio the right way round is 3:2; this is PN:AP.
traps.B: 1:1 would need M and N to be placed symmetrically; they are not.
traps.D: 2:1 is the ratio you get if N were the midpoint of OB.
traps.E: 3:1 uses ON:OB = 1:3 as ON:NB, confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole.
traps.F: 4:1 does not arise from these ratios.

questions.detail: Ratio at an intersection of cevians

questions.stem_html:
A fair coin is tossed 6 times.

What is the probability that no two heads occur on consecutive tosses?
questions.solution_html:
Count the sequences with no two adjacent heads. Let an be the number of such sequences of length n.

A valid sequence ends in T (any valid sequence of length n−1) or in HT (any valid sequence of length n−2). So an = an−1 + an−2 — the Fibonacci numbers.

a1 = 2, a2 = 3, then 5, 8, 13, 21.

Probability = 2164.

Listing all 64 sequences is possible and is what the question is testing you will not do. The recurrence takes fifteen seconds.

traps.A: 13/64 is a₅/2⁶ — the count for five tosses over the total for six.
traps.B: 1/4 is a guess-shaped answer with no count behind it.
traps.C: 5/16 = 20/64, one short: usually the all-tails sequence dropped.
traps.E: 27/64 counts sequences with at most one head, plus some.
traps.F: 1/2 would be the answer if the condition were vacuous.

questions.stem_html:
How many ordered pairs of integers (x, y) satisfy

x2 + y2 = 2025?
questions.solution_html:
2025 = 452, so (−45, 0), (45, 0), (0, −45), (0, 45) work at once — four already, which rules out 0.

Beyond those, look for x2 + y2 = 2025 with both non-zero. 272 + 362 = 729 + 1296 = 2025. So do (36, 27), and every sign and swap of those: 8 more.

Checking the rest of the range turns up nothing else, giving 12.

27-36-45 is 9 × (3-4-5). Spotting that the radius is a multiple of 5 and reaching for the Pythagorean triple is the difference between fifteen seconds and trying every square below 2025.

traps.A: There are solutions — (45, 0) for a start.
traps.B: The four axis points only — the (±27, ±36) family is missed.
traps.C: The eight off-axis points only, forgetting the four on the axes.
traps.E: 16 counts an extra family of four that does not exist.
traps.F: 20 assumes two off-axis triples rather than one.
